subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Misinformation Effect
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Misinformation Effect.

hook.text: Witnesses saw a car crash. When asked about 'the broken headlight,' many recalled one that never existed.

buildup.text: Loftus showed that questions with false details can alter what people remember seeing.

discovery.text: Memories aren't recordings. They update each time we recall them, absorbing new information.

twist.text: Even gentle questions reshape memory. 'How fast were cars going when they smashed?' raises speed estimates.

climax.text: Every retelling is a rewrite. Memory blends what happened with what you heard afterward.

quiz.question: What did Loftus's research reveal about memory?
options: Memories are perfect recordings of events

details.summary: The misinformation effect occurs when post-event information distorts memory of the original event. Suggestive questions, media reports, and conversations with others can overwrite accurate memories with false details that feel completely genuine.
details.whyItMatters: The misinformation effect undermines eyewitness testimony, the most trusted form of evidence in courts. Memories are not recordings; they are reconstructions vulnerable to contamination from any information encountered after the event.
takeaways: Post-event information can permanently alter original memories
People cannot distinguish genuine memories from implanted ones
Elizabeth Loftus's research transformed understanding of memory reliability

faq.question: How does the misinformation effect contaminate eyewitness memory?
faq.answer: After witnessing an event, exposure to leading questions, media coverage, or conversations with other witnesses introduces new details. These details become incorporated into the memory and feel indistinguishable from genuinely observed events.

faq.question: Can people tell the difference between real and implanted memories?
faq.answer: No. Studies show people are equally confident in genuine and implanted memories. They report vivid sensory details for events that never happened. Without external corroboration, there is no reliable internal signal distinguishing true from false memory.
